basic_info.headline: AI-Assisted Software Development · IT & Network Operations
basic_info.meta_description: Trace Dugar’s portfolio: AI-assisted software development, Python application modernization, and IT and network operations.
basic_info.description: I combine IT and network operations experience with AI-assisted software development. My current work focuses on Python, application modernization, and secure, maintainable systems. Network support, field troubleshooting, and technical documentation shape how I approach engineering: understand the requirements, investigate failures, protect data, and verify the results. My background also includes audio engineering and full stack JavaScript training.

case_studies.title: TanMar Safety Platform
case_studies.subtitle: AI-Assisted Modernization and Application Consolidation
case_studies.summary: Leading the AI-assisted modernization of a legacy safety-training application and several smaller HR applications into one bilingual web platform. The work spans architecture, historical-data migration, access controls, performance, and verification.
case_studies.status: Core workflows implemented in the test environment; production hardening underway.

sections.title: Project overview
paragraphs: I’m leading the AI-assisted development of the TanMar Safety Platform, bringing a legacy safety-training application and several smaller HR applications into a unified bilingual web system. The project combines application modernization, requirements analysis, database redesign, security controls, performance optimization, and production-readiness planning.

The goal is to consolidate employee training and related administrative workflows while preserving the business rules and historical records those systems depend on. SafetyExam, the legacy Xojo training application, provides a substantial part of the behavior being analyzed and modernized.

sections.title: Platform workflows
paragraphs: The employee experience covers assigned training, instructional media, randomized exams, signatures, results, retakes, and completion tracking. The management experience supports employee administration, role- and location-scoped dashboards, announcements, training maintenance, reporting, exports, and annual scheduling.

sections.title: Directing AI-assisted development
paragraphs: I use Codex as an AI development partner and direct the work through documented requirements, legacy-system evidence, and testable product contracts. My responsibilities include defining the problem, guiding architectural and implementation decisions, investigating discrepancies, and evaluating the resulting application against its requirements.

Understanding the existing systems is central to that process. I reconcile observed legacy behavior with source code, database evidence, and business requirements to establish what the consolidated platform must preserve. That evidence also provides a basis for evaluating AI-assisted changes.

items.title: Separate application responsibilities
items.description: Domain rules, API contracts, persistence, and frontend concerns are organized separately to support testing and maintainability.

items.title: Preserve historical compliance records
items.description: The PostgreSQL redesign and migration work account for existing training results, signatures, employee obligations, and bilingual relationships. Transactional migrations and explicit database-target checks provide safeguards around data changes.

items.title: Make training rules explicit
items.description: English and Spanish variants remain consistent across assignments, attempts, results, and completion credit. Scored exams and media-only training use distinct completion rules that preserve their respective score and signature requirements.

items.title: Enforce organizational access on the server
items.description: Authorization reflects employee, management, and administrator responsibilities, including role and location scope.

items.title: Optimize complete workflows
items.description: Dashboard and Training Matrix improvements address database queries, filtering, data transport, resource loading, and browser rendering while preserving search, keyboard, print, and export behavior.

sections.title: Verification and acceptance
paragraphs: The verification strategy combines Python unit and contract tests, frontend component and build-contract tests, and Playwright workflow coverage. Feature acceptance includes PostgreSQL-backed checks so that database-dependent behavior is tested against the platform’s database system. Documented requirements and verification evidence guide acceptance throughout the AI-assisted development process.

sections.title: Current status
paragraphs: Core employee, management, reporting, and training workflows are implemented in the authoritative test environment. Current work focuses on operational hardening, portable deployment configuration, and final physical-device and accessibility acceptance before a production rollout.

case_studies.title: Aquarium
case_studies.subtitle: An Experiment in Prompt-Only AI Development
case_studies.summary: An ongoing experiment in building and maintaining a Godot game through prompting alone. I direct the product, playtest, and critique results while AI agents perform implementation. Aquarium explores how durable context, scoped work, and independent verification support sustained AI development across sessions.
case_studies.status: Development preview; behavior, visual refinement, and performance work ongoing.
case_studies.imageAlt: October 2026 development screenshot of Aquarium’s live-rendered title screen with stylized fish and plants
case_studies.imageCaption: Aquarium title screen — October 2026 development preview.

sections.title: The experiment and the game
paragraphs: Aquarium asks whether a substantial game can be developed and maintained through prompting alone. The experiment deliberately excludes manual project edits by me: code, configuration, models, editor changes, repairs, and Git operations belong to AI agents.

The game itself is observation-first artificial life: a calm miniature world with persistent individuals and truthful recorded histories, without chores, scores, or an economy. Making that experience enjoyable provides a concrete product against which to evaluate the workflow.

sections.title: Cory foraging: a worked example
paragraphs: I requested a more readable corydoras foraging sequence: the mouth needed to reach the sand, disturb it, and transition into a short swim. AI implementation and independent checks exposed particle movement and turning defects. The team retained those failures and extended the correction to account for the fish’s body and fins during turns and settling.

A focused development fixture recorded 458 passing foraging checks; an unchanged shared-area departure test also passed for all six fish. Preserved reports, source inventories, and an independent correspondence review tie these historical results to the corrected development sequence. These are bounded checks, not universal collision-clearance acceptance. Broader species traffic remains work in progress.

video.title: Corydoras foraging — development diagnostic close-up
video.caption: Development diagnostic close-up: a four-second rendered witness using a separate camera and an extended foraging visit. It shows the corrected sequence; it is not a normal gameplay session or a performance benchmark.

sections.title: My role and the feedback loop
paragraphs: My tools are prompts, observation, playtesting, and critique. I make product and creative decisions, provide references, screenshots, logs, and feedback, and ask agents to investigate or change the project. They own implementation, tooling, debugging, builds, tests, and documentation.

Specialized responsibilities cover architecture, persistence, behavior, performance, and independent review. Written scopes and acceptance criteria turn feedback into bounded work; durable context carries decisions across sessions. My role is to direct that loop and judge the experience, while keeping unfinished experiments distinct from the installed preview.

sections.title: Routing the AI team to relevant context
paragraphs: I directed a scoped reorganization of the information used by the AI team. Agents begin with governance and current state, then follow a router to the relevant subsystem and exact contract. AI agents implemented the documentation changes while preserving original decisions, research, and evidence; runtime and unfinished features stayed outside the scope.

At the October 10 documentation checkpoint, mandatory startup reading fell from 5,228 to 2,543 whitespace-separated words, a 51.36% reduction. This measures that historical reading set, not present-day context size, token cost, productivity, or model reliability.

sections.title: State and persistence boundaries
paragraphs: Saved inhabitants carry identity, motion state, traits, and recorded histories. Save handling validates a complete candidate before adoption, uses staged writes and backups, and refuses unsupported future formats. Persistence changes receive explicit review because they affect the continuity of a player’s world.

The living title scene has a separate responsibility: its creatures are disposable presentation, with independent randomness and no saved individual history. The title’s species ensemble does not expand the persistent aquarium roster, which currently contains harlequin rasboras. This boundary protects the saved world while allowing visual experimentation.

sections.title: Original visuals through iteration
paragraphs: I direct a miniature diorama style with soft sculpted forms, tactile materials, and readable species silhouettes. Agents generate and refine the project’s creature models and materials through prompts. Anatomy and posture come before markings. Species references, matched camera and lighting comparisons, and playtesting guide fins, movement, contact, and habitat use. Biological research informs the design while its uncertainties remain documented. Geometry checks support review; visual and motion acceptance still require my judgment.

sections.title: Performance and tradeoffs
paragraphs: Performance work has focused on CPU fin deformation, repeated geometry queries, and scene workload. The preview includes an optional C++ fin backend that preserves the existing calculations, with the original GDScript implementation available as a fallback. Candidate changes are compared against frozen predecessors across creature variants and failure paths.

I keep workload changes separate from implementation gains when interpreting results. Source diagnostics, frame-time samples, and packaged-player behavior answer different questions; broader performance acceptance remains ongoing.

sections.title: Verification and independent review
paragraphs: The workflow records source and build identity, uses isolated test profiles, and preserves failed checks alongside successful evidence. Review asks whether a test measures its stated claim and whether the tested candidate matches the delivered build. Independent review complements automated checks; my playtesting covers qualities that need human judgment. Narrow passing results do not close unrelated behavior, visual, or performance gates.

One proposed contact-query optimization passed 69,634 sampled comparisons against a frozen predecessor. Independent AI static analysis then identified an unsampled boundary where the finer spatial index could change the result. The team rejected the optimization and restored the original index. The counterexample was analytical, not executed in Godot; this records a decision to reject adoption, not a demonstrated performance gain.

sections.title: Current status and next steps
paragraphs: Aquarium is an in-progress development preview with a live title habitat and a persistent aquarium path. Group routing for celestial pearl danios remains unfinished. Next work includes behavior corrections, broader contact and movement verification, visual refinement, and performance acceptance. The experiment remains ongoing: I’m evaluating how scoped prompts, durable context, and independent review support progress over time.

case_studies.title: Linux Ticket Generator & RHEL Lab
case_studies.subtitle: Designing a Stateful AI Workflow for Linux Operations Practice
case_studies.summary: A headless RHEL homelab paired with a stateful AI-guided Linux ticket generator. The workflow carries environment state, ticket history, and learning gaps across sessions. Two completed account and least-privilege exercises show how I use AI mentoring to investigate, make targeted changes, and document verification.
case_studies.status: RHEL lab configured; two Tier 1 account and permission exercises completed in May 2026.
case_studies.imageAlt: HP ProDesk hardware repurposed for the PaleHorse RHEL homelab
case_studies.imageCaption: Repurposed HP ProDesk hardware for the PaleHorse RHEL homelab.

sections.title: Project overview
paragraphs: I built a Linux practice environment around PaleHorse, my headless RHEL homelab, and designed an AI-guided ticket generator to make that environment useful for repeatable troubleshooting practice. The combination connects physical infrastructure work with AI workflow design: a real machine provides the baseline, while a documented simulation introduces realistic operational problems.
My goal was to practice judgment as well as commands. Each ticket presents symptoms and incomplete context, asks me to investigate, and ends with verification and a written resolution.

The worked examples below are controlled Tier 1 exercises completed on May 2, 2026: fictional accounts and deliberately seeded faults on the real lab server. Claude Code issued the scenarios; AI mentoring supported my diagnosis and command use.

sections.title: TICK-002: restoring an account’s interactive login
paragraphs: This exercise concerned a fictional developer account that could not complete an interactive login. The completion log identifies a nologin shell and missing home directory. My retained notes describe checking the account, investigating the missing home, and an initial mkdir/chown attempt. With AI mentoring, I learned how ownership and default home files work.

My resolution note records setting Bash, correcting the home with mkhomedir_helper, setting owner-only permissions (700), and testing SSH successfully. The retained account output below shows the Bash entry. The login result is documented in my closure note; no raw SSH success transcript survives.

transcript.title: Retained, user-pasted account output; real administrator and host redacted

sections.title: TICK-001: narrowing an account’s privileges
paragraphs: The initial id output showed a fictional junior-administrator account in wheel. The lab’s recorded sudoers policy granted that group unrestricted sudo access. With AI mentoring and the usermod documentation, I worked through a targeted membership change. My resolution note records removing the practice account; the later group listing shows only the lab administrator remaining.

The retained before-and-after inspection covers wheel membership, not a complete audit of alternative sudo grants. I also recorded the learning gaps exposed: connecting group membership with the configured sudo policy and checking the correct group file.

transcript.title: Retained, user-pasted inspection: before (id) and after (group listing); real administrator and host redacted
transcript.content:
<lab_admin>@<lab_host>:~$ id jrodriguez
uid=1001(jrodriguez) gid=1001(jrodriguez) groups=1001(jrodriguez),10(wheel)

<lab_admin>@<lab_host>:~$ grep wheel /etc/group
wheel:x:10:<lab_admin>

sections.title: Building the RHEL foundation
paragraphs: I repurposed an HP ProDesk 600 G2 with an upgraded i7-6700, 1 TB SSD, and 16 GB RAM. After installing RHEL and registering a developer subscription, I configured networking with nmcli, assigned a static address, enabled network auto-connect, and established SSH access from my workstation.

The setup involved diagnosing an inactive network interface and working around package availability limits by compiling btop from source. I documented installation, configuration, troubleshooting, and validation so the lab has an understandable baseline for later work.

sections.title: Designing the AI workflow
paragraphs: I use Claude Code as the scenario engine and learning mentor. The reusable /linux-ticket skill is instructed to read three persistent files before issuing one ticket: environment_state.md records the environment, ticket_log.md records completed exercises, and weak_areas.md guides targeted follow-up practice.

This makes continuity part of the design rather than relying on chat history. I provide and review the baseline, define the ticket and review formats, and evaluate the AI’s guidance. An early skill-loading problem also required correcting the directory structure to use a named folder containing SKILL.md.

sections.title: Design decisions and boundaries
paragraphs: The state model distinguishes real machine facts from simulated, planned, and unknown resources. That separation matters: a fictional permission problem should not become an assumed fact about the actual server. The documented progression covers nine areas, from users and permissions to mixed incidents, with one exercise at a time.

The workflow asks for read-only inspection, a reasoned diagnosis, a narrow fix, least privilege, and before-and-after checks. Higher-risk work calls for backups, disposable environments, or simulation. These are instructions for practice; human review remains necessary when evaluating AI suggestions or making system changes.

sections.title: Verification and resolution
paragraphs: For the RHEL setup, I documented connectivity checks, DNS resolution with dig, a successful SSH session, resource visibility through btop, and network accessibility after reboot. These checks establish the specific behavior tested during setup.

The documented closure process calls for inspecting the relevant state, explaining the change, verifying the intended result, and writing a resolution note. The review format includes environment changes and learning gaps for follow-up exercises.

sections.title: Lessons and next steps
paragraphs: The strongest lesson is that useful AI workflows need explicit state, clear responsibilities, and a way to check their output. A reusable skill reduces setup friction, while the journal preserves decisions and troubleshooting context. The hardware lab also reinforced the need to test remote access after reboot rather than assuming configuration persists.

These two completed exercises make the learning process visible: initial inspection, targeted changes with mentoring, retained output, and written closure. The next step is to carry the recorded gaps into further practice and strengthen verification. The linked GitHub journal contains the full setup and reusable workflow.

current_projects.title: Portfolio Recovery & Seaside Redesign
current_projects.summary: Recovered and refreshed my existing React portfolio through AI-assisted development, reconnecting its source to my current GitHub and Netlify deployment. A custom seaside design brings synchronized day/dusk lighting, bilingual content, responsive layouts, and keyboard-friendly project galleries into one coherent experience.
current_projects.description: I recovered my existing portfolio and reconnected its editable source to my current GitHub account and Netlify deployment. Working with Codex, I defined the visual direction, reviewed iterations, and refined the result into a miniature California seaside theme. The update extends the artwork through typography, locally hosted icons, project cards, About, and the timeline. It also improves English/Japanese content, routing, focus handling, and mobile layouts while preserving earlier project screenshots. Optimized assets and regression checks support ongoing maintenance. The gallery pairs updated views with before screenshots, and the public repository contains the implementation.

highlights.title: One shared animation clock
highlights.description: Day and dusk share a packed video and one wave clock. A 1.2-second cosine blend drives scene lighting and interface colors together, allowing theme changes without restarting the ocean motion.

highlights.title: Usability across languages and devices
highlights.description: I refined mobile navigation, route focus, keyboard galleries, and Japanese translations; reordered the timeline newest first; and removed retired demo links while retaining historical screenshots and surviving repository links.

highlights.title: Maintainable delivery
highlights.description: I kept the existing React foundation, optimized WebP images, self-hosted the font and icons, cached local content, and deferred project details. Regression tests and browser checks preceded Netlify publication.

current_projects.title: PaleHorse Intro Script
current_projects.summary: A custom Bash terminal intro for my RHEL machine, combining an ASCII horse, ANSI color, and readable system information. Built through hands-on scripting and AI-assisted iteration on layout, formatting, and terminal presentation.
current_projects.description: I created a custom terminal intro for PaleHorse, my RHEL machine, using Bash and AI-assisted iteration. The script clears the terminal, renders an ASCII horse and a red PaleHorse wordmark, then displays uptime, load averages, distribution, and version in aligned columns. It reads distribution metadata from /etc/os-release, parses uptime output with awk, and uses ANSI 256-color sequences and Bash string replacement to color the artwork. I directed the visual choices and refined formatting through repeated feedback. This small project explores readable terminal presentation and reusable shell formatting patterns. The public script and linked journal document the implementation and artwork sources.
